name: lexindex
baseline: XCDAT 15 (C++ compressed double-array trie dictionary) and MARISA (marisa-trie 0.2.6)
workload: Compressed string dictionary (string to dense id and back) over 13 corpora (Wikipedia titles, domains, PyPI names, paths, identifiers, UUIDs, DNA and others) at 1M and 10M keys; measures serialized bytes per key, single-key lookup latency, build time.
claimed_speedup: Smallest structure on 13 of 13 corpora at 1M keys against the campaign's MARISA and XCDAT builds (e.g. words 2.51 vs 2.98 B/key for MARISA rho=2; titles-en 7.21 vs 8.19). HashedDictIndex (closed) lookup 14 to 61 ns against XCDAT 15's 54 to 449 ns at 1M keys. Strict exact-search structures still trail XCDAT 15 on 9 of 13 corpora at 1M keys.
compiler_and_flags: C++ competitors (MARISA, XCDAT driver) built with c++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17 (-DNDEBUG for XCDAT and floor drivers) per harness/build.sh; GCC 16.2.1, rustc 1.98.1; lexindex 4.5.2 from crates.io
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800HS (8 cores / 16 threads), Fedora 44, measured 2026-09-26
tradeoffs: Immutable string-to-id indexes only. Seven index types trade size against speed: front-coded DictIndex is smallest but slowest to look up; HashedDictIndex adds a perfect hash for fast id lookup. Rust crate with Python bindings and a C ABI, so usable from C++ only through the C interface.
caveats: Harness author is the lexindex author (conflict of interest, disclosed in the README; harness pins every competitor and publishes JSON artifacts). The 14 to 61 ns closed HashedDictIndex lookup returns an id for keys that were never inserted, so it is not equivalent to the tries' exact search. Against MARISA at its smallest (1 to 32 tries, untimed) the size margin shrinks to 0.04 to 3.8 percent on paths and titles, and MARISA is smaller once loaded on five corpora. Size win is the main claim; speed wins are limited to the closed-lookup variant and a few corpora (dna, numeric). Baselines are succinct tries, not SDSL or sux directly (the C2 harness builds sdsl-lite and sux as dependencies only).
found_via: https://github.com/ilgrad/string-index-benchmarks (shootout README, found via search for compressed trie dictionary benchmarks marisa-trie darts-clone cedar xcdat)

name: xcdat (evidence from string-index-benchmarks)
baseline: MARISA (marisa-trie 0.2.6), also CoCo-trie, PDT, FST and C2 variants
workload: Exact-match lookup in compressed string dictionaries over 13 corpora at 1M keys, 6 corpora at 10M keys, single-key lookup latency in ns.
claimed_speedup: XCDAT 15 is the fastest other structure for exact lookup on every corpus at 1M keys (words 78 ns, dna 277 ns, domains 147 ns, titles-en 243 ns, urls 365 ns, uuid 339 ns); on words the README quotes MARISA rho=2 at 346 ns against XCDAT 15 at 78 ns (about 4.4x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: c++ -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -std=c++17, GCC 16.2.1, XCDAT pinned at commit 2451441
tradeoffs: XCDAT 15 is larger than MARISA or front-coded structures (words 7.30 B/key against MARISA rho=2's 2.98). Double-array trie, static dictionary only.
caveats: Independent third-party harness, but the harness author competes with their own library (lexindex). Tier A relies on public harness, stated compiler flags and CPU. Evidence for an already catalogued project; only the MARISA comparison row is used here.

name: C2 (cache-conscious succinct tries)
workload: Lookup latency and size of succinct tries (FST, CoCo-trie, MARISA families) over 6 key-set datasets; case IDs and scripts in run_benchmarks.sh.
claimed_speedup: C2-FST up to 1.92x faster and up to 41% smaller; C2-CoCo up to 1.22x faster and up to 46% smaller (against CoCo'); C2-MARISA up to 1.51x faster and up to 46% smaller.
compiler_and_flags: C++20 compiler (GCC 10 or later, Clang 12 or later), CMake Release build; exact flags not stated on the page
hardware: single Intel Xeon Gold core with 25 MB LLC (exact model not stated)
tradeoffs: Header-only research re-implementations that need Boost and vendored baselines (sdsl-lite, ds2i, sux, FSST) as submodules; build is involved. Adds adaptive unary-path compression and tail containers (FSST, Re-pair).
caveats: Numbers come from the authors' arXiv preprint (2606.16104, blocked here) and README; code is public but CPU model and compiler flags are partial, hence tier C. The listed repo is a public release copy of HardyZ1906/C2 (the page shows it as a fork); alexztc/C2 redirects here. Speedups are 'up to' maxima. The independent string-index-benchmarks harness rebuilds C2 variants and reports C2-CoCo rho=1 as the smallest competitor on dna at 10M keys.
found_via: WebSearch: compressed trie dictionary C++ benchmark marisa-trie darts-clone cedar xcdat; then https://github.com/ilgrad/string-index-benchmarks

name: AWFM-index (AvxWindowFmIndex)
workload: Exact-match count and locate k-mer queries on nucleotide and amino acid FM-indexes, thread-parallel.
claimed_speedup: Count 2 to 6x faster and locate 2 to 4x faster than SeqAn3's FM-index; roughly 2 to 4x for nucleotide and 2 to 6x for amino acid search (paper abstract and body as seen in search-result snippets only).
hardware: 32-core Intel Xeon E5-2630 v3 at 2.40 GHz, 64 GB RAM (from search snippet of the paper)
tradeoffs: Strided bit-vector layout using AVX2 (also ARM Neon) and an optional k-mer seed table that trades memory for speed; optional on-disk suffix array. Index is specialised for DNA/protein alphabets, not a general succinct-structure library. C library with C API, callable from C++.
caveats: Numbers were read from WebSearch snippets of the peer-reviewed Algorithms for Molecular Biology paper (doi 10.1186/s13015-021-00204-6); the paper pages (PMC, BMC) are blocked here, so snippet only. Compiler flags and benchmark code not confirmed. Tier C under the snippet-only rule; likely B or A after the paper is read. The README itself carries no numbers.
found_via: WebSearch: FM-index C++ library benchmark faster than sdsl-lite; then WebSearch for awfmindex and github page https://github.com/TravisWheelerLab/AvxWindowFmIndex

name: 3star-rankselect (3* rank/select)
baseline: SDSL, Poppy, rank9sel, pasta (compared in the repo's benchmark script)
workload: Rank and select on plain bit vectors with worst-case constant query time; repo script benchmarks select_1 query time (ns) and space overhead percent against competitor code it downloads.
claimed_speedup: Space overhead of 0.78 percent, 4.5x to 64.1x less overhead than previous implementations (search snippet of the paper abstract). Query-time ratios not seen.
tradeoffs: Targets minimal space overhead with worst-case constant-time queries; the README does not claim faster queries than pasta or SDSL, only 'good practical performance'.
caveats: Paper (arXiv 2509.17819, Kurpicz, Rigi-Luperti, Sanders) is blocked here; the abstract numbers come from a search snippet. The repo README reports no numbers; the benchmark script run_bitvectors.py logs t(ns) and overhead_percent but I could not run or see output. The claim is about space, not speed. Reproduction script fetches competitor code at first run.
found_via: WebSearch: Theory Meets Practice for Bit Vectors Supporting Rank and Select github

name: vers (vers-vecs)
baseline: Rust crates succinct (rank9), rsdict, bio, fid, indexed_bitvec, sucds, bitm; range_minimum_query and librualg for RMQ
workload: Bit-vector rank and select, Elias-Fano access and predecessor, and range-minimum queries versus other Rust crates, plus heap overhead of the bit vector.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative: 'among the fastest publicly available bit vector implementations for rank and select'; 'substantially lower memory overhead than alternatives'; 'outperforms both [RMQ crates] by a significant margin'; BMI2/popcnt intrinsics speed rank and select by 2 to 3x. The succinct crate is faster on rank. Results are SVG plots, no numeric table on the page.
compiler_and_flags: target-cpu=native, simd feature enabled (requires AVX-512), rsdict simd feature on nightly Rust
tradeoffs: Pure Rust crate; not usable from C++ without bindings. SIMD feature needs AVX-512 and unsafe code. Wavelet matrix, Elias-Fano, BP tree included.
caveats: Compares only against other Rust crates, not SDSL or sux, so it does not beat the named baselines of this category. Benchmark repo (Cydhra/vers_benchmarks) has no README and its results are plots, so no numbers were verified. Included as shootout context for Rust succinct libraries.

name: pasta::bit_vector (evidence from bit_vector_experiments)
baseline: CS-Poppy; experiments repo also builds sdsl-lite, sux, splatlab rankselect and rankselect2 as competitors
workload: Rank and select queries on plain bit vectors; space overhead of the rank/select index.
claimed_speedup: pasta-flat has 3.51 percent space overhead; the SIMD flat variant answers rank up to 8 percent and select up to 16.5 percent faster than CS-Poppy (README summary and search snippet of the SPIRE 2022 paper).
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 licence limits reuse; C++20 header-only; AVX2 versions for best speed.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. Reproduction code is public at https://github.com/pasta-toolbox/bit_vector_experiments (submodules sux, sdsl-lite, rankselect, rankselect2, tlx), but I could not see results, CPU or flags (paper at arXiv 2206.01149 blocked). Gains over SDSL are not quoted on the pages I opened; the quoted percentages are against CS-Poppy.
